title: Web Crawler
prompt: Design a polite, deduplicating web crawler at internet scale. Given a seed list, the crawler should fetch and store the HTML of every reachable page on the public web. Target ~1B pages crawled per month, respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Fetch HTML, extract links, store, recur. Respect robots.txt. Don't drift into search indexing or ranking.

must: Fetch HTML for a given URL
Discover new URLs from fetched pages
Respect robots.txt and per-domain rate limits
should: Avoid re-crawling unchanged pages too often
avoid: Designing the search index — that's a different system

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Given a URL, fetch the HTML and store it.
2. Extract outbound links from each fetched page and enqueue them.
3. Respect robots.txt and per-domain crawl-delay rules.
4. Avoid fetching the same URL twice within a refresh window.
5. Detect near-duplicate content and skip storing it twice.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: Throughput, politeness, fault tolerance, storage scale, freshness. Quantify.

must: Fault tolerance — single fetcher failure must not lose URLs
should: Freshness target — recrawl interval per content type
Extensibility for new content types (RSS, sitemaps)
avoid: Forgetting politeness — the most common failure mode of bad crawler designs
Promising consistency on a globally-distributed crawl frontier

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Throughput: ~400 pages/sec sustained (1B / 30d ≈ 386).
- Politeness: max 1 concurrent request per host, default 1 req/sec unless robots.txt specifies otherwise.
- Fault tolerance: any single fetcher / parser failure does not lose URLs in flight.
- Storage: avg 100KB/page → ~100TB/month, ~1.2PB/year.
- Freshness: news domains recrawled daily; long-tail every 30 days.
- Eventual consistency on the URL frontier is fine.

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: URL, Page (the fetched content), Frontier (the queue), HostPolicy.

avoid: Mixing the queue and the storage as one entity

stages.sampleAnswer:
- URL: { url, priority, discoveredAt, lastFetchedAt? }
- Frontier: priority queue of URLs to fetch, partitioned by host.
- HostPolicy: cached robots.txt + crawl-delay per host.
- Page: { url, fetchedAt, status, contentHash, html }.
- LinkGraph: outbound links extracted, used to rediscover.

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: Crawler is mostly internal — there's an admin API for seeds and metrics, plus internal queues. Don't over-spec REST.

must: Internal queue protocol described (even if not REST)
avoid: Inventing user-facing APIs the system doesn't need

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the components and walk through the fetch path.
stages.howToAnswer: Frontier → fetcher pool → parser → URL filter → dedupe → storage. Show how host politeness is enforced. Show the recursive discovery loop.

must: Distributed frontier partitioned by host (so politeness is local to one worker)
Fetcher pool that respects per-host rate limit
Dedupe before re-enqueue (URL seen-before? content seen-before?)
should: Bloom filter for cheap URL-seen check
avoid: Single-process queue that doesn't scale horizontally

stages.sampleAnswer:
Frontier: Kafka topic, partitioned by host hash → each fetcher consumer is responsible for a stable subset of hosts. This is the key trick — it means politeness can be enforced in-process without distributed locks.

Fetcher pool (1000s of stateless workers): for each URL, check the in-memory robots.txt cache (refresh every 24h). Apply the host crawl-delay (sleep if needed). Fetch via HTTP client with timeouts. Publish 'page fetched' event with raw HTML to a Kafka topic.

Parser (separate worker pool): consumes 'page fetched' events. Extracts outbound links. Normalizes URLs (strip fragments, canonical case, sort query params). Publishes 'link discovered' events.

URL filter: dedupe via a sharded Bloom filter — if probably-seen, drop. Otherwise compute hash, check authoritative seen-set in a sharded KV store, write-through, enqueue back into the frontier.

Content dedupe: SHA-256 of normalized HTML. If we've already stored a page with this hash, just record the additional URL pointing at it.

Storage: HTML compressed and written to S3 (one object per page, keyed by content hash). Metadata in Cassandra keyed by URL.

stages.title: Deep Dives
stages.questionPrompt: Harden against the hardest problems: spider traps, freshness, JavaScript-rendered pages.
stages.howToAnswer: Pick 2-3 of: spider traps, freshness scheduling, JS rendering, sitemap usage, 404 handling, IP rotation.

must: A spider-trap defense (max depth or per-host page cap)
A freshness strategy that doesn't recrawl everything uniformly
should: JavaScript rendering for SPAs (separate worker pool with headless browsers)
Adaptive recrawl based on observed change rate
avoid: Recrawling every page on a fixed cadence (wastes most of the budget)

stages.sampleAnswer:
Spider traps: cap pages-per-host (e.g., 100K) and per-page outbound links (1K). Detect URL patterns where the path keeps growing (`/cal/2024/01/15/event/foo/cal/2024/01/16/...`) and stop following them.

Freshness: each URL has a recrawl-after-timestamp. We schedule based on observed change frequency — pages whose content hash changed last time get shorter intervals; static pages get pushed to 30+ days. News-domain hostnames are tagged 'high freshness' and get a 1-day floor.

JS rendering: 90% of pages don't need it. We render only pages tagged as SPAs (detected by zero text outside <script> tags after initial fetch) on a separate, expensive headless-Chrome worker pool. Otherwise we'd burn 100x the compute for marginal gain.

Sitemaps: when fetching robots.txt, also fetch sitemap.xml. Treat its URLs as priority-elevated seeds.
